Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set, let $(S_i,\mathcal S_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces, set $S=\prod_{i\in I}S_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra, and let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $S$. For a nonempty block $B\subseteq I$, write $S_B=\prod_{i\in B}S_i$, $S_{-B}=\prod_{i\in I\setminus B}S_i$, let $p_{-B}:S\to S_{-B}$ be the coordinate projection, and define $\pi_{-B}(D):=\pi(p_{-B}^{-1}(D))$ for measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$.

Products and product sigma-algebras use the empty-product convention in [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: if $B=I$, then $S_{-B}$ is the one-point space $\{()\}$ with its trivial sigma-algebra.

A **proper full conditional kernel** for block $B$ is a supplied probability kernel $K_B:S_{-B}\to S_B$ such that for every product-measurable $C\subseteq S$ and every measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$,
$$\pi\bigl(C\cap p_{-B}^{-1}(D)\bigr)=\int_D K_B(z,C_z)\,\pi_{-B}(dz),\qquad C_z:=\{u\in S_B:\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)\in C\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)$ is the unique state whose coordinates on $I\setminus B$ are $z$ and whose coordinates on $B$ are $u$. This is the event-identity definition of a regular conditional distribution of the block given the retained coordinates, with every kernel section a probability measure at every $z$. It makes no existence claim; the A-page density corollary gives one sufficient case.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The quadratic form of $\Sigma$ is $(a,b)\Sigma(a,b)^T=(\sigma_Xa+r\sigma_Yb)^2+(1-r^2)\sigma_Y^2b^2$, so it is positive for every nonzero $(a,b)$; also $\det\Sigma=\sigma_X^2\sigma_Y^2(1-r^2)>0$. Its inverse is $\Sigma^{-1}=\frac1{\sigma_X^2\sigma_Y^2(1-r^2)}\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_Y^2&-r\sigma_X\sigma_Y\\-r\sigma_X\sigma_Y&\sigma_X^2\end{pmatrix}$. Thus [F2] applies. Substitution into its density formula, using [F3] to identify the product reference measure, gives $p(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_X\sigma_Y\sqrt{1-r^2}}\exp[-\frac{u^2-2ruv+v^2}{2(1-r^2)}]$. The covariance convention in [F1] fixes the parameters used here.

Set $s_X=\sigma_X\sqrt{1-r^2}$, $s_Y=\sigma_Y\sqrt{1-r^2}$, $a(y)=m_X+r\sigma_Xv$, and $b(x)=m_Y+r\sigma_Yu$. For $s>0$ write $g_{c,s}(t)=s^{-1}\phi((t-c)/s)$. The identities $u^2-2ruv+v^2=(u-rv)^2+(1-r^2)v^2=(v-ru)^2+(1-r^2)u^2$ therefore give both factorizations $p(x,y)=g_{m_Y,\sigma_Y}(y)g_{a(y),s_X}(x)=g_{m_X,\sigma_X}(x)g_{b(x),s_Y}(y)$. Expanding each squared term verifies the exponents, and multiplying the factors verifies the prefactors.

For any $c\in\mathbb R$, $s>0$, and Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, the diffeomorphism $T(t)=c+st$ in [F4] gives $\int_A g_{c,s}(z)\,dz=\int_{T^{-1}(A)}\phi(t)\,dt=N(c,s^2)(A)$ by [F5]. Thus each $g_{c,s}$ is a probability density. Applying [F6] to the first factorization in step 2.1 yields $m_Y(y)=\int p(x,y)\,dx=g_{m_Y,\sigma_Y}(y)$; the second factorization gives $m_X(x)=\int p(x,y)\,dy=g_{m_X,\sigma_X}(x)$. These marginal densities are finite and strictly positive at every real argument.

Apply [F7] to $p$ with Lebesgue reference measures and, for each updated coordinate, the supplied filler $N(0,1)$ from [F5]. Since both marginal densities in step 3.1 are finite and positive everywhere, the density formula is used on every conditioning fibre. For measurable $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, the first conditional kernel is $K_X(y,A)=\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,dx}{m_Y(y)}=\int_Ag_{a(y),s_X}(x)\,dx=N(a(y),s_X^2)(A)$, using the factorization in step 2.1 and density identification in step 3.1. Exchanging coordinates gives $K_Y(x,A)=N(b(x),s_Y^2)(A)$. By [F7] these are probability kernels satisfying the conditional event identities; [F8] identifies them as proper full conditionals at every conditioning value. The proof makes no assertion at the excluded singular endpoints.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set, let $(S_i,\mathcal S_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces, set $S=\prod_{i\in I}S_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra, and let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $S$. For a nonempty block $B\subseteq I$, write $S_B=\prod_{i\in B}S_i$, $S_{-B}=\prod_{i\in I\setminus B}S_i$, let $p_{-B}:S\to S_{-B}$ be the coordinate projection, and define $\pi_{-B}(D):=\pi(p_{-B}^{-1}(D))$ for measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$.

Products and product sigma-algebras use the empty-product convention in [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: if $B=I$, then $S_{-B}$ is the one-point space $\{()\}$ with its trivial sigma-algebra.

A **proper full conditional kernel** for block $B$ is a supplied probability kernel $K_B:S_{-B}\to S_B$ such that for every product-measurable $C\subseteq S$ and every measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$,
$$\pi\bigl(C\cap p_{-B}^{-1}(D)\bigr)=\int_D K_B(z,C_z)\,\pi_{-B}(dz),\qquad C_z:=\{u\in S_B:\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)\in C\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)$ is the unique state whose coordinates on $I\setminus B$ are $z$ and whose coordinates on $B$ are $u$. This is the event-identity definition of a regular conditional distribution of the block given the retained coordinates, with every kernel section a probability measure at every $z$. It makes no existence claim; the A-page density corollary gives one sufficient case.

**Inputs:** The finite product state space and target law from [[def-gibbs-full-conditional-kernel]], a nonempty block $B$, its supplied proper full conditional kernel $K_B$, and a current state $x\in S$.

**Output:** A new state $x'\in S$ whose retained coordinates equal $x_{-B}$ and whose updated block is sampled from $K_B(x_{-B},\cdot)$.

The transition kernel is
$$P_B(x,C)=\int_{S_B}\mathbf1_C\!\left(\operatorname{splice}_B(x_{-B},u)\right)K_B(x_{-B},du),\qquad C\in\mathcal S.$$
Operationally, retain every coordinate outside $B$, draw $u$ from the full conditional kernel at the retained value, and replace the coordinates in $B$ by $u$. The finite product sigma-algebra makes the splice map measurable; the kernel-integral theorem makes the displayed evaluation measurable in $x$. The well-definedness result is [[lem-gibbs-block-update-is-a-probability-kernel]].

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$

Operationally, retain every coordinate outside $B$, draw $u$ from the full conditional kernel at the retained value, and replace the coordinates in $B$ by $u$. The finite product sigma-algebra makes the splice map measurable; the kernel-integral theorem makes the displayed evaluation measurable in $x$. The well-definedness result is [[lem-gibbs-block-update-is-a-probability-kernel]].

Let $E$ be a finite nonempty state space and $p$ a transition matrix on $E$. A subset $C\subseteq E$ is **closed** when $\sum_{y\in C}p(x,y)=1$ for every $x\in C$. The finite chain is **reducible** when it has a nonempty proper closed subset. This definition is the only reducibility convention used by the finite-support example on this page.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set, let $(S_i,\mathcal S_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces, set $S=\prod_{i\in I}S_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra, and let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $S$. For a nonempty block $B\subseteq I$, write $S_B=\prod_{i\in B}S_i$, $S_{-B}=\prod_{i\in I\setminus B}S_i$, let $p_{-B}:S\to S_{-B}$ be the coordinate projection, and define $\pi_{-B}(D):=\pi(p_{-B}^{-1}(D))$ for measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$.

Products and product sigma-algebras use the empty-product convention in [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: if $B=I$, then $S_{-B}$ is the one-point space $\{()\}$ with its trivial sigma-algebra.

A **proper full conditional kernel** for block $B$ is a supplied probability kernel $K_B:S_{-B}\to S_B$ such that for every product-measurable $C\subseteq S$ and every measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$,
$$\pi\bigl(C\cap p_{-B}^{-1}(D)\bigr)=\int_D K_B(z,C_z)\,\pi_{-B}(dz),\qquad C_z:=\{u\in S_B:\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)\in C\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)$ is the unique state whose coordinates on $I\setminus B$ are $z$ and whose coordinates on $B$ are $u$. This is the event-identity definition of a regular conditional distribution of the block given the retained coordinates, with every kernel section a probability measure at every $z$. It makes no existence claim; the A-page density corollary gives one sufficient case.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Assume AC. Let $m_X,m_Y\in\mathbb R$, let $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y>0$, and let $-1<r<1$. Put
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_X^2&r\sigma_X\sigma_Y\\r\sigma_X\sigma_Y&\sigma_Y^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \pi=N_2\bigl((m_X,m_Y),\Sigma\bigr).$$
Then proper full conditional kernels of $X$ given $Y=y$ and of $Y$ given $X=x$, at every real conditioning value, are
$$X\mid Y=y\sim N\!\left(m_X+r\frac{\sigma_X}{\sigma_Y}(y-m_Y),\,\sigma_X^2(1-r^2)\right),\qquad Y\mid X=x\sim N\!\left(m_Y+r\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x-m_X),\,\sigma_Y^2(1-r^2)\right).$$
Both conditional variances are strictly positive. The singular cases $|r|=1$ are not included.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

**Inputs:** The finite product state space and target law from [[def-gibbs-full-conditional-kernel]], a nonempty block $B$, its supplied proper full conditional kernel $K_B$, and a current state $x\in S$.

**Output:** A new state $x'\in S$ whose retained coordinates equal $x_{-B}$ and whose updated block is sampled from $K_B(x_{-B},\cdot)$.

The transition kernel is
$$P_B(x,C)=\int_{S_B}\mathbf1_C\!\left(\operatorname{splice}_B(x_{-B},u)\right)K_B(x_{-B},du),\qquad C\in\mathcal S.$$
Operationally, retain every coordinate outside $B$, draw $u$ from the full conditional kernel at the retained value, and replace the coordinates in $B$ by $u$. The finite product sigma-algebra makes the splice map measurable; the kernel-integral theorem makes the displayed evaluation measurable in $x$. The well-definedness result is [[lem-gibbs-block-update-is-a-probability-kernel]].

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $-1<\rho<1$ and let $\pi=N_2(0,\Sigma_\rho)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, where
$$\Sigma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Writing the state as $(X,Y)$, its proper full conditionals are
$$X\mid Y=y\sim N(\rho y,1-\rho^2),\qquad Y\mid X=x\sim N(\rho x,1-\rho^2) \quad (x,y\in\mathbb R).$$
The variances are positive for every allowed $\rho$, so each conditional is a pointwise probability kernel on the whole conditioning space. A systematic scan that updates $X$ and then $Y$ can be run by the two corresponding updates of [[alg-gibbs-block-update]].

Let $m\ge1$ and let $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ be exact block-update kernels for the same target probability $\pi$. Under the chronological composition convention of [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels]], the systematic full-sweep kernel $P_1\cdots P_m$ leaves $\pi$ invariant. It need not be reversible.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel on $(S,\mathcal S)$ and let $\pi$ be a probability measure on that space. The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$**, or satisfies **detailed balance**, when
$$\int_A P(x,C)\,\pi(dx)=\int_C P(y,A)\,\pi(dy)\qquad(A,C\in\mathcal S).$$
This is the symmetry of the two-time transition flow $\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$, stated through its values on measurable rectangles. The definition is for a general measurable state space and makes no irreducibility, uniqueness, or convergence assertion. Invariance means $\int P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal S$, as in [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]].

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

For probability kernels $K:(S,\Sigma)\to(T,\Tau)$ and $L:(T,\Tau)\to(U,\Upsilon)$, their **composition**, in the order K then L, is
$$(KL)(s,A)=\int_T L(t,A)\,K(s,dt),\qquad s\in S,\quad A\in\Upsilon.$$

The kernel convention is [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The integrand is measurable in t and lies in $[0,1]$, so the displayed number exists in $[0,1]$. As a function of s it is measurable by [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], applied to the product-measurable function $(s,t)\mapsto L(t,A)$: its threshold preimages are rectangles $S\times\{t:L(t,A)>a\}$. The probability-kernel assertion and associativity are justified by [[lem-kernel-composition-is-well-defined-and-associative]].

Composition refers to specified pointwise kernels. Almost-everywhere classes alone do not define this formula until representatives and the relevant measures are specified. For an empty source the candidate is the empty map. No choice of versions or assumption of AC enters this definition.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: The conditional means in [F1], integrated in the order [F6] under the joint law [F5], give $\mathbb E X_1=\rho\mathbb E Y_0=0$ and $\mathbb E Y_1=\rho\mathbb E X_1=0$. By [F8], the initial target has $\mathbb E Y_0^2=1$ and $\mathbb E[X_0Y_0]=\rho$. The first conditional variance in [F1] gives $\mathbb E[X_1^2\mid Y_0]=\rho^2Y_0^2+1-\rho^2$, so $\mathbb E X_1^2=1$. The invariant full-sweep law [F2] gives $(X_1,Y_1)\sim\pi$, hence $\mathbb E Y_1^2=1$. Thus all four coordinates are square-integrable, and their cross-products are integrable by $2|ab|\le a^2+b^2$.

The means in step 1.1 are zero, so [F4] makes each cross-covariance equal to its product expectation. Using the kernel order [F6], the first conditional mean in [F1], and [F8], $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,X_1)=\int\pi(dx_0,dy_0)y_0\int x_1K_1(y_0,dx_1)=\rho\mathbb E Y_0^2=\rho$. For the other cross term, the second conditional mean followed by the first gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,Y_1)=\int\pi(dx_0,dy_0)x_0\int K_1(y_0,dx_1)\int y_1K_2(x_1,dy_1)=\rho^2\mathbb E[X_0Y_0]=\rho^3$. The integrability established in step 1.1 justifies these signed iterated integrals.

If the full-sweep kernel were reversible, [F3] would give equality of its two-time law and the state-swapped measure on every rectangle. Both are finite measures, so [F7] gives equality on the product sigma-algebra. The integrable function $((x_0,y_0),(x_1,y_1))\mapsto y_0x_1$ would then have the same integral as its state-swapped version $x_0y_1$, forcing $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,X_1)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,Y_1)$ because all four coordinates are centered. But [F8] and step 2.1 give these covariances as $\rho$ and $\rho^3$, which differ for $\rho=\tfrac12$. Hence the full-sweep kernel is not reversible, although [F2] proves it preserves $\pi$.
